strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: extending error slice discovery from image-level classification to instance-level tasks (object detection and segmentation), where failures stem from spatial, contextual, and relational factors.

Proposes a well-motivated generate-and-verify framework (GH-ESD) that combines top-down LLM knowledge with bottom-up grounded captioning, and introduces a monotonic sensitivity trend test that effectively mitigates VLM hallucinations compared to rigid error-rate thresholding.

Contributes GESD, a substantial and meticulously annotated benchmark for instance-level slice discovery comprising 42 expert-defined error slices across 12K images with 1500 hours of human verification.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple dimensions, including GESD instance-level tasks, standard image-level bias benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++), and actionable downstream model repair (GroupDRO on Faster R-CNN).
weaknesses: The dataset refinement procedure in Step 4 artificially overwrites non-slice errors with ground-truth predictions to create 'perfect' non-slice instances. While this isolates the target slices for evaluation, it removes realistic background error noise that could potentially confound statistical verification in real-world open-world settings.

The multi-stage pipeline relies heavily on high-capacity LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro) and VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) for captioning, attribute inference, and scoring, but the main text lacks discussion of computational overhead, API token costs, and wall-clock latency required to evaluate large datasets.

In Section 5.2, the comparison between hypotheses and atomic tags relies on an LLM evaluator (Gemini-2.5-Pro) to judge semantic alignment with ground-truth slices, which risks LLM evaluator bias or self-preference.

Although segmentation is highlighted as a primary instance-level task in the title, abstract, and dataset description, the main text focuses almost exclusively on detection, relegating segmentation quantitative results to the supplementary material.

strengths: Important and under-explored problem: Most existing error slice discovery works focus on image-level classification and spurious correlations. Extending slice discovery to instance-level tasks (object detection and segmentation) addresses relational, contextual, and spatial failure modes critical for real-world deployments.

Principled framework design: The generate-and-verify formulation cleanly bridges top-down world knowledge (LLM) and bottom-up region evidence (VLM). Formulating verification as a monotonic trend test over continuous matching scores provides a sound statistical defense against VLM hallucinations and noisy subgroup thresholding.

Valuable benchmark contribution (GESD): The authors introduce a dedicated instance-level slice discovery benchmark constructed from COCO, KITTI, and face detection datasets with substantial manual annotation effort (1500 person-hours, 42 expert-defined slices across detection and segmentation), providing a standardized ground truth for future research.

Comprehensive experimental validation and model repair: GH-ESD consistently outperforms baseline approaches on GESD (P@10 improves from 0.63 to 0.73) and generalizes well to classic image-level benchmarks. The practical utility is demonstrated via model repair (e.g., GroupDRO reweighting improving bicycle detection mAP from 28.58 to 33.59).
weaknesses: Artificial dataset refinement: In Step 4 of the GESD benchmark construction, model predictions outside defined slices are overwritten with ground truth to create 'synthetic perfect' non-error regions. While this isolates evaluation to predefined slices, it simplifies the error landscape compared to real-world deployment where spurious correlations and unmodeled errors coexist.

Reliance on adapted baselines: Because existing slice discovery techniques (FACTS, HiBug, etc.) were primarily designed for image-level classification or atomic tag combinations, all comparisons on GESD rely on adaptations. While the authors put commendable effort into fair adaptations (including upgrading models to GPT-5.2 and Gemini), it highlights the nascent nature of instance-level slice discovery baselines.

Evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge: In Section 5.2, evaluating semantic alignment between discovered hypotheses and ground-truth slices relies on Gemini-2.5-Pro. Although prompt templates are provided in the supplementary material, LLM evaluator bias could affect precision/recall assessments.

Computational overhead and scalability: Querying VLMs for per-instance grounding across large pools of candidate hypotheses and evaluation units (FNs, FPs, discrepancies) can incur substantial computational and inference costs. A discussion of runtime and token/API cost trade-offs in the main text is missing.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Extends slice discovery from image-level classification and global attribute biases to instance-level vision tasks (object detection and segmentation), where errors are often driven by relational and spatially localized visual contexts.

Technically sound framework: The generate-and-verify formulation using continuous VLM matching scores paired with monotonic performance sensitivity verification is principled, mitigating VLM hallucination and noisy empirical thresholding.

Valuable benchmark contribution: Introduces GESD, covering over 12K images from COCO, KITTI, and face detection datasets with 42 expert-annotated grounded error slices, filling a clear void in standardized instance-level slice discovery evaluation.

Thorough evaluation: Demonstrates consistent improvements over adapted baselines (FACTS*, HiBug, HiBug2) on GESD, provides meaningful ablation studies dissecting each component, demonstrates generalization on classic image-level benchmarks, and verifies actionable utility via model repair experiments.
weaknesses: Artificial dataset refinement: In Section 4 (step 4), model predictions not belonging to any defined error slice are overwritten with ground truth to create 'perfect' annotations for non-error parts. While this isolates target slices, it removes real-world detector noise and background false positives, which may simplify the retrieval setting compared to real deployment conditions.

LLM-as-a-judge evaluation circularity: In the semantic relevance ablation (Section 5.2), Gemini-2.5-Pro is employed to evaluate whether discovered hypotheses match ground truth slices. Since Gemini-2.5-Pro is also the backend used for hypothesis generation in GH-ESD, this evaluation strategy risks self-preference or evaluation bias.

Underrepresented segmentation analysis in the main paper: Although instance segmentation is repeatedly highlighted in the abstract and introduction as a primary target task, almost all quantitative and qualitative results in the main text focus on object detection, with segmentation results deferred to the supplementary material.

Computational overhead and scalability: Evaluating every candidate evaluation unit (proposals, predictions, and ground-truth boxes) against multiple hypotheses using a 7B VLM introduces considerable inference cost, which warrants a more explicit discussion of computational overhead and scalability in the main text.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in model evaluation and debugging: extending error slice discovery from image-level classification to spatially grounded, instance-level vision tasks (object detection and instance segmentation).

The proposed GH-ESD framework is technically sound and well-formulated, effectively combining top-down knowledge-driven priors with bottom-up grounded caption extraction, continuous probabilistic VLM matching scores, and monotonic trend-based statistical verification to filter out spurious hallucinations.
Introduction of GESD, a substantial and rigorously curated benchmark with 42 expert-defined failure slices and extensive human annotations across COCO, KITTI, and face detection datasets.

Strong empirical results across both instance-level tasks (GESD detection and segmentation) and image-level benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++), consistently outperforming prior representation-clustering and attribute-tagging baselines.

Demonstrates practical actionability through model repair experiments (e.g., substantial +5.0 mAP improvement on bicycle detection using slice-aware GroupDRO reweighting) and provides an interactive user interface tool for real-world inspection.
weaknesses: The dataset refinement procedure for GESD (Section 4, Step 4) artificially overwrites non-slice errors with ground-truth predictions to create 'perfect' background annotations. While this isolates the predefined slices for evaluation, it removes natural background error noise and makes the evaluation scenario somewhat synthetic compared to real-world messy deployment.

The semantic alignment ablation in Section 5.2 uses an LLM (Gemini-2.5-Pro) to judge semantic relevance between predicted hypotheses and ground-truth error slices. Using LLM-as-a-judge without human cross-validation on this specific metric risks inheriting model-specific evaluation biases.
Section 5 states that baselines were reproduced using 'GPT-5.2', which appears to be a typo or placeholder that requires correction and clarification.

Computational overhead and scalability: running VLM-based grounded inference and captioning over all candidate evaluation units (TPs, FPs, FNs) across large-scale datasets remains computationally demanding, which could limit real-time or continuous testing workflows.

strengths: Important problem formulation: The paper effectively addresses a key limitation in existing error slice discovery research, extending it from image-level classification to instance-level vision tasks (object detection and segmentation) where failures often stem from contextual, relational, and spatial factors.

Sound technical framework (GH-ESD): The generate-and-verify approach thoughtfully combines knowledge-driven (top-down LLM) and data-driven (bottom-up grounded VLM) hypothesis generation. Using continuous VLM token logit matching coupled with a monotonic performance sensitivity test (sliding-window slope / Spearman rank-correlation) provides a principled way to filter out VLM hallucinations and spurious slices without relying on arbitrary fixed error-rate thresholds.

High-effort benchmark construction (GESD): Introducing GESD provides an annotated benchmark with 42 expert-defined, spatially grounded error slices across detection and segmentation (leveraging COCO, KITTI, and face datasets with ~1,500 person-hours of verification).

Comprehensive empirical validation: GH-ESD consistently outperforms existing embedding- and tag-based baselines (e.g., HiBug2, FACTS) across Precision@k on GESD, shows solid generalization to image-level benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++), provides detailed ablation experiments, and proves actionable downstream utility through model repair via GroupDRO.
weaknesses: Artificial dataset refinement: In Section 4 (Step 4), model predictions for instances not belonging to any defined error slice were overwritten with ground truth to create a synthetic 'perfect' non-error baseline. While this isolates evaluation to predefined slices, it simplifies the noise profile of real-world detector outputs where confounding, open-world false positives and false negatives naturally co-occur.

Requirement of ground truth for evaluation units: Constructing the evaluation units U requires explicit prediction-ground truth matching (categorizing into TP, FP, FN, and localization discrepancy). This restricts the framework's direct applicability to curated validation datasets and limits its utility in unannotated production/monitoring environments.

Computational overhead and scalability: Although employing locally hosted Qwen2.5-VL with vLLM mitigates external API costs and latency, running instance-grounded VLM queries across thousands of candidate bounding boxes and open-ended hypothesis spaces is significantly more compute-intensive than feature-space clustering methods.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Extending error slice discovery from image-level classification to instance-level vision tasks (object detection and segmentation) addresses an important gap in trustworthy computer vision and failure analysis.

Grounded hypothesis generate-and-verify paradigm: Leveraging LLM semantic priors and VLM region-level grounding to generate structured natural-language hypotheses overcomes the expressiveness limitations of atomic bag-of-tags and latent embedding clustering.

Benchmark contribution (GESD): Creating a dedicated benchmark comprising 42 expert-defined failure hypotheses across COCO, KITTI, and face detection datasets represents a substantial annotation effort (1,500 person-hours).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper includes comparative experiments against adapted baselines (FACTS, HiBug2), ablation studies on grounding and verification components, and testing on standard classification bias benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++).
weaknesses: Flawed statistical definition of monotonic trend: In Section 3.4, the trend statistic is defined as Trend(h) = max_{w in W} slope_w over sliding windows. Taking the maximum slope across localized windows (some containing as few as 5 samples) does not establish a consistent monotonic relationship across hypothesis intensity. Any localized noisy spike can produce a high positive slope and pass the threshold, contradicting the claim of testing consistent monotonic error sensitivity.

Unrealistic synthetic dataset refinement: In Section 4 (Step 4), model predictions on all instances not belonging to any defined error slice were artificially overwritten with ground truth. This reduces the background error rate outside the 21 target slices to zero, eliminating open-world distractor failures and creating an artificially clean testbed that inflates slice discovery precision compared to real-world deployment settings.

Evaluation protocol and slice selection bias: Precision@k is evaluated by selecting the 'Best Predicted Slice' for each ground-truth slice (Table S3). Because methods generate vastly different numbers of candidate slices (e.g., HiBug2 generates 3,666 slices while GH-ESD generates 102), evaluating solely on the post-hoc best match without penalizing false discovery across the entire generated slice set provides an incomplete and potentially biased assessment of discovery precision.

Limited scope and missing side-effect evaluation in model repair: The object detection repair experiment in Section 5.4 evaluates only a single slice ('bicycle partially occluded by a person') and reports metrics exclusively for the bicycle class (mAP-bicycle). The paper does not report overall COCO mAP across all classes, leaving it unverified whether slice-targeted reweighting degrades performance on other categories or exhibits negative transfer.
